idiom_name: GORM model struct + db.Create / db.Save / db.Delete
implementation_notes: GORM is the dominant Go ORM and its model is the Active Record idea without inheritance: a struct embeds gorm.Model (ID, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, DeletedAt) to inherit identity and timestamps, and persistence methods live on the *gorm.DB handle - db.Create(&u) inserts and back-fills the primary key, db.Save(&u) updates by primary key, db.Delete(&u) soft-deletes when DeletedAt is present, and hooks such as BeforeCreate/AfterCreate put row-local logic on the model. What replaces the classic base class is struct embedding plus package-level methods, and the escape hatch to a data mapper is a query builder (sqlc, sqlx, squirrel) over database/sql, which is where Go teams usually go once queries outgrow CRUD.
code_sketch:
type User struct {
    gorm.Model
    Name string
    Age  int
}
u := User{Name: "Jinzhu", Age: 18}
db.Create(&u)      // INSERT ...; u.ID back-filled
u.Age = 19
db.Save(&u)        // UPDATE users SET ... WHERE id = u.ID
var got User
db.First(&got, u.ID)
pitfalls: Zero values are ambiguous: by default GORM will not write zero-value fields (0, "", false) for columns with a default tag, so pointer or sql.Null* types are needed to persist them.
Save writes every column of the struct, so an instance built from a form overwrites fields it never loaded; Updates with a map or Select narrows the write.
There is no implicit transaction across calls - several Save calls in one request must be wrapped in db.Transaction, and sessions must not be reused concurrently without care.
